title: Psychological Safety
text:
In the 1990s, Amy Edmondson, then a doctoral student at Harvard, studied 51 work teams in a manufacturing company that made office furniture. They ranged from sales and production teams to management groups. She combined surveys of team members, interviews and her own observations, and gathered ratings of each team's performance from managers and internal customers.

Her focus was a quality she called psychological safety: a shared belief in the team that it is safe to take interpersonal risks. In such teams, people do not expect to be embarrassed, rejected or punished for asking a question, admitting an error, asking for help or raising a concern.

Edmondson found that teams with higher psychological safety engaged more in what she called learning behavior. They sought feedback, discussed mistakes openly, asked for help and tried out new ideas. That learning behavior, in turn, was linked to better team performance. Team leaders who coached and were accessible tended to have safer teams. In interviews, members of low-safety teams described keeping quiet about problems and choosing not to ask questions so as not to look ignorant or incompetent.
lesson: Teams improve only when people can admit what they do not know. Make it normal to ask questions and report mistakes, starting with your own.
location: A manufacturing company in the United States
source: Edmondson, A. (1999). Psychological safety and learning behavior in work teams. Administrative Science Quarterly, 44(2), 350-383.
